title: Cooking indoors in a winter outage: what is safe
summary: Which cookers you can use inside in a winter outage, and which kill. A vented wood stove or fireplace is best; gas range burners and chafing fuel need a window open and a CO alarm, and are for cooking only. A butane cassette stove is the same only if its label allows indoor use; if not, it goes outside. Charcoal, barbecues, camp stoves, generators and an oven left on for heat stay out.

steps.text: Before you light anything, have a battery CO alarm working outside the sleeping rooms (Health Canada CO, CDC winter), and ideally a second near where you cook.
Cook on what is vented first: the top of a wood stove or cookstove, or a fireplace with a working chimney (CDC winter, Ready.gov food).
On a gas range with no power, hold a lit match beside a surface burner and turn the knob to low. Keep every burner either lit or off (GE match lighting).
steps.warn: Gas flows from a burner that is on but not lit (GE match lighting). If one blows out, turn it off and air the room before relighting.

steps.text: Open a window close to the stove before you light it, and keep it open until the cooking is done (Health Canada cooking).
Stand chafing fuel on a tray that won't burn, about 1 m (3 ft) from anything that will, with a lid or snuffer at hand (UC Berkeley chafing fuel). Use a cassette stove only as its own card describes.
Turn every burner off when the food is done. Never run a burner or the oven to heat the room (CDC power outage, CDC winter).
steps.warn: An oven or burner left on for warmth puts CO into the room (CDC power outage, CDC winter).

steps.text: Do all other cooking outside: camp stoves, barbecues and charcoal. A generator stays outside too, 6 m (20 ft) from the house, with only its cord coming in (Health Canada CO, CDC winter).

notes:
## The short answer

Every flame makes carbon monoxide. What decides whether a cooker is safe inside is where its exhaust goes. A wood stove or fireplace sends it up a flue. A gas range, a chafing can or a cassette stove puts it into the room, so they need a window open and a CO alarm, and you run them only while you cook. Anything built for outdoors stays outdoors.

| Method | Indoors? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Top of a wood stove or wood cookstove | Yes | Vented to outside through its chimney; its fumes go up the flue only if the flue is sound and clear (CDC winter). See [Cooking on a wood stove](#guides/skill_cook_on_wood_stove) |
| Fireplace with a working chimney | Yes, with care | Listed as an emergency cooking source (Ready.gov food); use only one that vents properly (CDC winter) |
| Gas range-top burners | Yes, for cooking only, with a window open and a CO alarm | Light with a match in an outage (GE match lighting). Burners put CO and NO2 into the room: open a window nearby (Health Canada cooking) and keep a CO alarm working (Health Canada CO) |
| Gas oven, or any oven with the door open, for heat | Never | Never use a gas range or oven to heat a home (CDC power outage). GE says its gas ovens can't be lit with a match because the igniter and gas valve need power (GE outage) |
| Chafing fuel, canned heat, fondue burner | Yes, with ventilation, cooking only | Chafing dishes and fondue pots are on Ready.gov's emergency cooking list (Ready.gov food); the fuel burns in the room, so keep a window open and the CO alarm working |
| Butane cassette stove | Only if its label allows indoor use; cooking only | Many are made to a camp-stove standard for outdoor use only (CPSC butane report, Health Canada butane), so cook outside unless the label says otherwise. Where used at home, it is with an exhaust fan and windows open (HK CO case 2026). See [Cassette stoves](#guides/safety_cassette_stove) |
| Electric hot plate, kettle or slow cooker on a generator or battery | Yes | No flame indoors; the generator itself stays outside, 6 m (20 ft) from the house (Health Canada CO) |
| Propane, white-gas or multi-fuel camp stove | No | Makers say outdoor use only, never in a house, camper or tent (Coleman propane stove, MSR WhisperLite) |
| Charcoal grill, hibachi, gas barbecue | No | Never inside a home, tent or camper (CDC power outage, CDC winter) |
| Generator, even in a garage with the door open | No | Never indoors; 6 m (20 ft) from buildings (Health Canada CO) |

## Gas range in an outage

Most gas cooktops with electric spark ignition still work in a power cut: hold a lit match beside the burner and turn the knob to low (GE match lighting). Gas keeps flowing to a burner that is turned on but not lit, so keep every burner either burning or off (GE match lighting). The oven is different: its glow-bar igniter and gas valve need electricity, so it can't be lit by hand, and an oven that was on when the power went out stays off (GE outage). Check your own range's manual: some models differ.

A gas burner adds nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and moisture to the room. Health Canada's advice is to run the range hood fan, preferably on high, and to open a window close by if you have no hood (Health Canada cooking). In an outage the hood is dead, so the window is all you have. Crack it before you light up and keep it open until the pot is off. Use the back burners when the hood works (Health Canada cooking).

Never leave the burners or the oven on to warm the house. CDC is blunt: turning on the stove for heat is not safe (CDC winter), and never use a gas range or oven to heat a home (CDC power outage).

## Chafing fuel and canned heat

Ready.gov's list of emergency cooking sources includes chafing dishes, fondue pots and candle warmers (Ready.gov food). The small cans of gel or wick fuel that heat them burn in the room, so treat them as an open flame:

- Stand the can on something that won't burn: a baking sheet, pie pan or ceramic tile (UC Berkeley chafing fuel).
- Keep paper, napkins, plastic and cloth about 1 m (3 ft) away (UC Berkeley chafing fuel).
- Keep the lid or a snuffer at hand and put the flame out as soon as you are done (UC Berkeley chafing fuel).
- Light it with a long match or long lighter, never move it while lit, and let a used can cool before you take it out (BU chafing fuel).

They give little heat. They are for warming food and slow simmering, not for boiling a big pot.

## Outdoor-only cookers

Camp stoves, barbecues and charcoal are cheap, plentiful and tempting in a cold kitchen. They are built for open air. Coleman's propane camp stove manual says it is for outdoor use only and never inside a house, camper, tent or vehicle (Coleman propane stove). MSR's liquid-fuel stove manual says the same and adds that it must be used only to boil water or cook food (MSR WhisperLite). Coleman also notes that storing or using propane cylinders larger than about 1 lb (0.45 kg) inside occupied buildings is unsafe and illegal in some places (Coleman propane stove).

Cook outside on them, or under an open-sided shelter well away from doors and windows, then carry the food in. A rocket stove does the same job on twigs: see [Rocket stove](#guides/build_rocket_stove).

## Signs something is wrong

- Headache, dizziness or nausea in the kitchen, or in several people at once: turn everything off and get outside. See [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).
- A CO alarm that sounds, even once.
- A yellow, sooty flame on a gas burner instead of a blue one, or stuffy air and condensation on the windows where something is burning (see the [CO hazard card](#browse/hazards/co_gas)).

## Before the outage

Find a battery CO alarm and fresh batteries now. Health Canada ranks the hallway outside the sleeping rooms as the most important place for one (Health Canada CO); a second near where you will cook warns you sooner. The test button checks the alarm's electronics, power and horn, not the sensor (First Alert test). Learn how your range lights by hand while the lights are still on (GE match lighting). Keep a box of long matches by the stove. One more alarm limit: Kidde rates its alarms for 40 to 100 °F (about 4 to 38 °C), so check the range on yours, because a cold kitchen in an outage can sit below it (Kidde temperature). See [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide) for expiry dates and the low-level silence.
